text.p: THE PROTEUS COLUMN
Demutalisation of insurers is generating much interest, largely focused on the windfall it can bring to policyholders and the share opportunities demutualisations present to the stockmarket.

In Britain, the flotation of Norwich Union has advertising campaigns tempting lucky punters to spend their money on new kitchens, holidays or double glazing, while personal finance journalists advise applying for extra shares because they will soar in value.

But the path to demutualisation is not always easy. In Massachusetts, a proposed bill would allow conversion of a mutual to a holding company that has 51 percent controlling stock interest in a stock insurer that is created. The idea is that this would permit the state's insurance industry to remain competitive without a negative impact on policyholders.

Although well supported by the industry, there are real problems over jurisdiction. Not only would many of the firms base themselves in Delaware, the fact that the new mutual holding companies wouldn't be engaged in the business of insurance creates other problems. Federal securities laws, federal antitrust laws and federal bankruptcy laws may apply and the state's exclusive jurisdiction to regulate may well be eliminated.

In Australia, as the AMP Society prepares for its $12-billion Australian dollar stockmarket listing, it will first have to deal with the bitter legacy of a decision to call in more than 200 million Australian dollars in loans to its agents.
Australian media have reported that as many as 50 of the agents have been bankrupted, some after more than 20 years of service.

The Australian Financial Review described the situation as a warning to anyone dealing with a big corporation -- pointing out that changes in strategy and personnel can destroy small businesses that have grown too reliant on the organisation.

Agents had been a tradition in Australia for generations. They were at the core of AMP's growth and its strong reputation in the community. Agents wrote the policies that created the 12 billion Australian dollars in reserves that are now the capital base of the proposed float. Even today, agents account for 90 percent of AMP's retail sales.

AMP has confirmed that since 1991 it has been involved in legal action with 64 of its agents, and there is outstanding legal action against 29. If any of these cases creates a precedent of damages against AMP, it could cause a big headache in the lead-up to the public float.
